## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Study Context

Armed conflict in Myanmar dates back to independence in 1948. It has largely been fought between ethnic armed organisations and the national armed forces, the Tatmadaw, over self-determination and the federalisation of the country. Ceasefires and the self-administered zones created in 2008 did not end these demands, and the conflict is often described as the longest ongoing civil war in the world.

In February 2021, the military seized power from the government elected in 2020, which was led by the National League for Democracy. Repression of protests, marked by arbitrary arrests and indiscriminate violence, intensified the conflict rather than ending it. Many civilians fled to forests and mountainous areas, others joined armed resistance, and large areas slipped almost entirely out of the junta's control. Violence since 2021 has therefore been uneven across the country, which makes the question of where it concentrates, and how that is changing, a spatial one.

### 1.2 Purpose and Objectives

This exercise analyses armed conflict in Myanmar, measured through political violence, at the township level from 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025. The data is drawn from two sources: event data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) and township boundaries from the Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU).

The analysis applies two spatial methods:

- **Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA)**, which identify townships where violence is unusually high or low compared with neighbouring townships.
- **Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)**, which tracks how hot spots and cold spots form, persist or fade over time.

In this study, political violence is defined following ACLED as "the use of force by a group with a political purpose or motivation, or with distinct political effects" (ACLED, n.d.). The exact scope of included events is set out in the Data and Study Design section.

The objectives are:

1.  To pinpoint exact geographic hot spots, cold spots and spatial outliers where violence clusters or behaves unusually compared with surrounding townships.
2.  To reveal where, how fast and in what pattern political violence is evolving over space and time.

### 1.3 Research Questions

1.  Is political violence spatially clustered across Myanmar's townships, or is it distributed randomly?
2.  Which townships are statistically significant hot spots, cold spots or spatial outliers?
3.  Where is political violence intensifying, persisting or fading, how fast it is happening, and in what pattern?
4.  What do these patterns imply for peace-building and conflict prevention?

## 2 Overview of Analytical Methods

### 2.1 Spatial Autocorrelation

Spatial autocorrelation is the degree to which values at nearby locations resemble one another. It follows from Tobler's (1970) first law of geography, which states that near things are more related than distant things. Similar values close together give positive spatial autocorrelation, while contrasting values close together give negative spatial autocorrelation. Measures of spatial autocorrelation are grouped by the scale at which they operate.

**Global indicators** summarise the whole study area in a single value. Moran's I (Moran, 1950) tests whether the pattern of values across townships differs from a random arrangement. It shows whether spatial dependence exists, but not where it is concentrated, so it is used first as a check on whether a local analysis is justified.

**Local indicators** give one result for each location. Local Moran's I, a local indicator of spatial association (LISA), compares each township with its neighbours and labels it as part of a high-high or low-low cluster, or as a spatial outlier (Anselin, 1995). The Getis-Ord Gi\* statistic (Getis & Ord, 1992; Ord & Getis, 1995) measures how strongly high or low values are concentrated in a township together with its neighbours, which identifies hot spots and cold spots. Both measures depend on how neighbours are defined through spatial weights, and significance is assessed by permutation.

### 2.2 Emerging Hot Spot Analysis

Measures of spatial autocorrelation describe only a single snapshot in time. Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) adds time by combining Gi\* with a trend test (Esri, n.d.). Events are first aggregated into a space-time cube of townships by time bins. Gi\* is then computed for each time bin, and the Mann-Kendall test (Kendall, 1975; Mann, 1945) checks whether each township's series of Gi\* values is rising or falling. By evaluating a township's hot or cold spot history alongside this trend, the analysis categorises it into a specific temporal pattern, such as new, consecutive, persistent, intensifying, diminishing, sporadic or oscillating.

## 3 Data and Study Design

### 3.1 The Data

| Dataset | Description | Format | Source |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **ACLED Myanmar Event Data** (January 2021 to September 2025) | Event-level records of political violence, protests and strategic developments, with date, location, event classification and fatality fields. | CSV | [ACLED](https://acleddata.com/) |
| **Myanmar Township Boundaries** (MIMU v9.4) | Township-level administrative boundaries for Myanmar, with state, district and township names and codes. | Shapefile | [MIMU](https://geonode.themimu.info/) |

### 3.2 Study Area and Period

The study area is **Myanmar**, and the unit of analysis is the township. The study period runs from **1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025**.

To capture how the spatial pattern of political violence has changed over time, the study period is also divided into different phases, anchored by two milestones that shaped the trajectory of political violence. On 7 September 2021, the National Unity Government declared a "people's defensive war" against the military (Al Jazeera, 2021). On 27 October 2023, the Three Brotherhood Alliance launched Operation 1027 in northern Shan State, a major coordinated offensive against the military (IISS, 2023).

| Phase | Months | Length |
|---|---|---|
| Coup and crackdown | January 2021 to August 2021 | 8 months |
| Armed resistance | September 2021 to October 2023 | 26 months |
| After Operation 1027 | November 2023 to September 2025 | 23 months |

::: {.callout-note}
While January 2021 precedes the 1 February coup, it is retained in the first phase to maintain data continuity. Similarly, October 2023 is kept in the second phase, as Operation 1027 did not begin until 27 October.
:::

### 3.3 Scope of Political Violence

In this study, the scope of armed conflict is determined by the disorder type that ACLED assigns to each event. ACLED groups events under three primary disorder types: "Political violence", "Demonstrations" and "Strategic developments". Notably, one sub-event type ("excessive force against protesters") carries two labels - "Political violence; Demonstrations" (ACLED, n.d.). For this analysis, all events labelled "Political violence" (including those with the dual label) are retained. This ensures alignment with the objectives of the study, and using ACLED's predefined classification for this filtering provides a documented, reproducible methodology.

| ACLED Disorder Type | Event Types (Sub-event Types) | Events | Inclusion Status |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Political violence | Battles; Explosions/Remote violence; Violence against civilians; Riots (mob violence) | 54,028 | Included |
| Political violence; Demonstrations | Protests (excessive force against protesters) | 261 | Included |
| Demonstrations | Protests (peaceful protest, protest with intervention); Riots (violent demonstration) | 14,987 | Excluded |
| Strategic developments | Strategic developments (for e.g., agreement, arrests, changes to group activity, etc.) | 17,833 | Excluded |

## 4 Setup

### 4.1 Installing and Loading the R Packages

The following R packages are used:

| Package | Purpose | Use Case in this Exercise |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **tidyverse** | Collection of packages for data import, manipulation and visualisation | Importing the ACLED data, wrangling and aggregating events, and producing the exploratory charts |
| **sf** | Imports, manages and processes vector-based geospatial data | Importing the township boundaries, converting event coordinates to spatial points, and joining events to townships |
| **sfdep** | Spatial dependence analysis within a tidy workflow | Building the spatial weights and the space-time cube, computing Local Moran's I and Gi\*, and running Emerging Hot Spot Analysis |
| **spdep** | Spatial weights and statistics for spatial dependence | Global Moran's I tests and the spatial correlogram |
| **tmap** | Thematic map creation using a layered grammar of graphics | Mapping event patterns, clusters and EHSA classes |
| **Kendall** | Mann-Kendall trend test | Testing the trend in each township's Gi\* series in Emerging Hot Spot Analysis |

```{r}
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, sfdep, spdep, tmap, Kendall)
```

### 4.2 Reproducibility

A fixed seed value of 123 is set for reproducibility of any simulation-based procedure used later in this study.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
```

## 5 Data Preparation and Quality Assessment

### 5.1 Importing the Data

#### 5.1.1 Myanmar Township Boundaries

The township boundary shapefile is imported with `st_read()` of **sf**:

```{r}
mmr <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
               layer = "mmr_polbnda_adm3_250k_mimu_1")

glimpse(mmr)
```

The following code chunk checks whether the township code is a unique key and whether all geometries are valid.

```{r}
mmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(townships = n(),
            unique_codes = n_distinct(TS_PCODE),
            unique_names = n_distinct(TS))

sum(!st_is_valid(mmr))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
All 330 township codes are unique, but only 328 township names are. In addition, all geometries were checked and found to be valid.
:::

The shared names are listed below:

```{r}
mmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(TS) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(TS, TS_PCODE, DT, ST) %>%
  arrange(TS)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The names Htantabin and Minhla each refer to two different townships located in separate districts and states.

Hence, `TS_PCODE` is used as the unique join key throughout, with township names reserved only for labels.
:::

#### 5.1.2 ACLED Event Data

The event file is imported with `read_csv()` of **readr**:

```{r}
acled <- read_csv("data/aspatial/ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv")
```

The following code chunk summarises the basic dimensions and data integrity checks for the imported ACLED dataset.

```{r}
tibble(
  check = c("Events", "Variables", "First event date", 
            "Last event date", "Duplicated event IDs", 
            "Missing coordinates"),
  result = c(nrow(acled), ncol(acled),
             as.character(min(acled$event_date)),
             as.character(max(acled$event_date)),
             sum(duplicated(acled$event_id_cnty)),
             sum(is.na(acled$latitude) | is.na(acled$longitude)))
)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The file contains 87,109 events and 31 variables. The first and last event dates (1 January 2021 and 30 September 2025) match the study period, and there are no duplicated event identifiers or missing coordinates.
:::

### 5.2 Spatial Join of Events to Townships

Events are assigned to townships by their coordinates. The event table is first converted to point features with `st_as_sf()`. Then, each point is matched to the township polygon that contains it with `st_join()`, using `st_within` as the join predicate. Only the township code is retained.

```{r}
acled_sf <- acled %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

acled_join <- st_join(acled_sf, mmr["TS_PCODE"], join = st_within)
```

The row counts before and after the join are compared to ensure that no events were lost or duplicated.

```{r}
c(before_join = nrow(acled_sf),
  after_join = nrow(acled_join),
  duplicated_ids = sum(duplicated(acled_join$event_id_cnty,)),
  unmatched = sum(is.na(acled_join$TS_PCODE)))
```

All 87,109 events are retained and none is duplicated. However, 15 events fall in no township polygon. The distance from each of them to the nearest township is measured:

```{r}
unmatched <- which(is.na(acled_join$TS_PCODE))
nearest <- st_nearest_feature(acled_join[unmatched, ], mmr)
dist_km <- as.numeric(st_distance(acled_join[unmatched, ],
                                  mmr[nearest, ],
                                  by_element = TRUE)) / 1000

acled_join[unmatched, ] %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(distance_km = dist_km,
         admin3_agrees = admin3 == mmr$TS[nearest]) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(events = n(),
            admin3_agrees = sum(admin3_agrees, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_km = round(max(distance_km), 2))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The 15 unmatched events fall into two groups. Nine are coded to Myanmar and lie within 0.64 km of a township boundary, so they are most likely points that sit near to a township edge. The township named in `admin3` (ACLED's third administrative level) matches the nearest township in all nine cases. These events are therefore assigned to their nearest township.

The remaining six events are coded to the Indian Ocean and lie approximately 642 km from the nearest township. None of these records have a matching `admin3`, providing no basis for placing them in a township. These events are therefore excluded.
:::

The adjustments to the 15 unmatched events are applied below:

```{r}
snap <- acled_join$country[unmatched] == "Myanmar"
acled_join$TS_PCODE[unmatched[snap]] <- mmr$TS_PCODE[nearest[snap]]

acled_join <- acled_join %>%
  filter(!is.na(TS_PCODE))

nrow(acled_join)
```

After the adjustments, **87,103 events** remain, each linked to exactly one township.

### 5.3 Data Quality Assessment

The township-linked events are assessed for locational reliability and coverage before the space-time cube is built.

#### 5.3.1 Cross-Validation of Township Assignments

ACLED records the township name of each event in `admin3`. This name is compared with the MIMU township that each event falls in.

```{r}
acled_join %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  left_join(mmr %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS),
            by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  summarise(blank_admin3 = sum(is.na(admin3) | admin3 == ""),
            compared = sum(!is.na(admin3) & admin3 != ""),
            agreement_pct = round(mean(admin3 == TS, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 1))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
`admin3` is blank for 1,112 events, which are excluded from the comparison. Among the remaining 85,991 events, the recorded township matches the MIMU township for 98.9%. The high agreement rate validates the approach of assigning events to townships based on their coordinates.
:::

#### 5.3.2 Geographic Precision

ACLED's `geo_precision` records how exactly an event is located:

```{r}
acled_join %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  left_join(mmr %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS),
            by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  group_by(geo_precision) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            pct = round(n / nrow(acled_join) * 100, 1),
            compared = sum(!is.na(admin3) & admin3 != ""),
            agreement_pct = round(mean(admin3 == TS, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 1))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Based on the output, approximately 56.6% of events are located at an exact site (level 1), 43.0% at a nearby location (level 2), and 0.4% within a broader area (level 3). The recorded township name agrees with the assigned township for at least 98% of compared events at every level, indicating that lower precision does not weaken the township assignment. Therefore, events of all precision levels are retained.
:::

#### 5.3.3 Political Violence Coverage

Political violence is the conflict variable analysed, and its coverage across townships is checked.

```{r}
pv <- acled_join %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(grepl("Political violence", disorder_type))

nrow(pv)

mmr %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  left_join(count(pv, TS_PCODE, name = "events"), by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  summarise(townships = n(),
            with_events = sum(!is.na(events)),
            without_events = sum(is.na(events)))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Following the spatial join, a total of 54,284 events meet the definition of political violence, forming the final sample size for this analysis. Across Myanmar's 330 townships, 322 recorded at least one event, while the remaining eight recorded none.
:::

#### 5.3.4 Temporal Coverage

The monthly number of political violence events is checked for gaps across the study period, since every time slice of the space-time cube requires data.

```{r}
pv_month <- pv %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(event_date, "month")) %>%
  count(month, name = "events") %>%
  complete(month = seq(as.Date("2021-01-01"),
                       as.Date("2025-09-01"),
                       by = "month"),
           fill = list(events = 0))

pv_month %>%
  summarise(months = n(),
            empty_months = sum(events == 0),
            min = min(events),
            median = median(events),
            max = max(events))
```

The monthly series is plotted below:

```{r}
milestones <- tibble(
  date  = as.Date(c("2021-02-01", "2021-09-07", "2023-10-27")),
  label = c("Military coup", "NUG declares\n'defensive war'", "Operation 1027")
)

ggplot(pv_month, aes(x = month, y = events)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(data = milestones, aes(xintercept = date),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(data = milestones, aes(x = date, y = Inf, label = label),
            vjust = 1.2, hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Political violence events per month") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
All 57 months record at least one event, confirming there are no temporal gaps in the data set. Monthly counts start at 65 in January 2021, rise sharply through the year to approximately 1,000, and stabilise around that level throughout 2022. In November 2023, the monthly count reaches its highest point at 1,473 events, after which it returns to approximately 1,000 per month by 2025. The median monthly count of political violence events is 993.
:::

### 5.4 Building the Space-Time Cube

A space-time cube holds one value for every township in every time slice. The cube is built from political violence events counted by township and month.

#### 5.4.1 Selecting the Time Bin

The time bin sets the temporal resolution of the space-time cube. To decide between a monthly or quarterly approach, the two methods are compared across the entire study period based on the number of resulting time slices and the sparsity of the data.

```{r}
compare_bins <- function(bin_unit, last_start) {
  pv %>%
    mutate(period = floor_date(event_date, bin_unit)) %>%
    count(TS_PCODE, period, name = "events") %>%
    complete(TS_PCODE = mmr$TS_PCODE,
             period = seq(as.Date("2021-01-01"), 
                          as.Date(last_start), 
                          by = bin_unit),
             fill = list(events = 0)) %>%
    summarise(bin = bin_unit,
              slices = n_distinct(period),
              rows = n(),
              zero_cells_pct = round(mean(events == 0) * 100, 1),
              mean_events = round(mean(events), 1))
}

bind_rows(compare_bins("month", "2025-09-01"),
          compare_bins("quarter", "2025-07-01"))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The output shows that monthly bins give 57 time slices, but 50.3% of township-months record no events, with an average of 2.9 events per cell. Quarterly bins give 19 time slices, with 30.7% of township-quarters remaining empty and an average of 8.7 events per cell.

Despite the sparser counts, **monthly bins** are selected for this analysis. They give each township a longer series for the Mann-Kendall test, and they allow changes in spatial patterns to be located to the month, which is essential for answering how fast political violence is evolving.
:::

#### 5.4.2 Aggregating Events to Township-Months

Events are aggregated by township and month. A space-time cube requires a value for every township in every month, so any township-month combination without recorded events is added to the table with a count of zero.

```{r}
pv_tm <- pv %>%
  mutate(month = floor_date(event_date, "month")) %>%
  count(TS_PCODE, month, name = "events") %>%
  complete(TS_PCODE = mmr$TS_PCODE,
           month = seq(as.Date("2021-01-01"), 
                       as.Date("2025-09-01"), 
                       by = "month"),
           fill = list(events = 0))
```

The completed table is checked for its size and the total number of events:

```{r}
pv_tm %>%
  summarise(rows = n(),
            total_events = sum(events))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The completed table has 18,810 rows (330 townships by 57 months) and a total of 54,284 events. This exactly matches the baseline count computed under the Political Violence Coverage subsection.
:::

#### 5.4.3 Creating the Time Series Cube

The space-time cube is created with `spacetime()` of **sfdep**, which combines the aggregated event table with the township boundaries. `TS_PCODE` serves as the location identifier and `month` as the time column.

```{r}
pv_st <- spacetime(pv_tm,
                   mmr %>%
                     st_transform(32647) %>%
                     select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST) %>%
                     arrange(TS_PCODE),
                   .loc_col = "TS_PCODE",
                   .time_col = "month")
```

Next, `is_spacetime_cube()` verifies that the object is a valid cube:

```{r}
is_spacetime_cube(pv_st)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The output is `TRUE`, confirming that every township has a value in every month. Hence, the cube is complete.
:::

## 6 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

### 6.1 Composition of Political Violence Events

Political violence comprises several event types. The chart shows the number and share of events by type:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

pv %>%
  count(event_type, sub_event_type) %>%
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n),
         label = paste0(format(n, big.mark = ","), " (",
                        ifelse(pct < 0.1, "<0.1", round(pct, 1)), "%)")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = reorder(sub_event_type, n), 
             fill = event_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.35))) +
  labs(x = "Number of events", y = NULL, fill = "Event type")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Political violence is highly distributed, with no single sub-event type accounting for a majority of incidents. Armed clashes are the most frequent (38.2%), followed by air/drone strikes (14.6%), remote explosives/IEDs (14.1%), attacks on civilians (13.9%), and shelling/artillery (12.5%). Other event types, such as excessive force against protesters (261 events) and mob violence (23 events), make up a small fraction of the total data.
:::

### 6.2 Political Violence Events by Township

The total number of political violence events per township, from 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025, is obtained by summing the monthly counts.

```{r}
mmr_events <- mmr %>%
  left_join(pv_tm %>%
              group_by(TS_PCODE) %>%
              summarise(events = sum(events)),
            by = "TS_PCODE")
```

The distribution of the counts is summarised below:

```{r}
mmr_events %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(min = min(events),
            q1 = quantile(events, 0.25),
            median = median(events),
            mean = round(mean(events), 1),
            q3 = quantile(events, 0.75),
            max = max(events))

ggplot(mmr_events, aes(x = events)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Political violence events per township", y = "Townships") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The summary statistics and histogram reveal that the distribution of political violence across townships is heavily right-skewed. While the median township experienced 80.5 events, the mean is significantly higher at 164.5, with the maximum reaching 1,058 events. This indicates that political violence in Myanmar is not uniformly distributed and requires the use of spatial cluster analysis to pinpoint where those intense concentrations occur.
:::

### 6.3 Spatial Distribution of Events

The total number of political violence events per township is mapped to show where events are concentrated.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

tm_shape(mmr_events) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "events",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", 
                                              n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Events")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The highest class (266 to 1,058 events) is concentrated in the central part of the country and along the southern strip, while the lowest two classes (0 to 53 events) are mostly in the north and east. High-count townships often sit next to each other, which suggests spatial clustering. However, this visual impression needs to be validated using local spatial statistics. The classes are quantiles, so each holds about the same number of townships, and the class ranges widen sharply towards the top.
:::

## 7 Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation

This section evaluates whether political violence events exhibit spatial dependence across townships, meaning that townships with similar event counts tend to be located near each other. Global Moran's I measures the degree of this spatial autocorrelation for the country as a whole, before the local patterns are examined.

### 7.1 Spatial Weights

Spatial weights define which townships are neighbours and how strongly they influence each other.

#### 7.1.1 Coordinate Reference System

The township boundaries are projected from WGS 84 to UTM zone 47N (EPSG: 32647), which covers central Myanmar. This converts the coordinate system so that distances are calculated in metres rather than degrees.

```{r}
mmr_utm <- st_transform(mmr_events, crs = 32647)
```

#### 7.1.2 Choice of Neighbours

Neighbours can be defined in three main ways:

- **Contiguity:** Defines neighbours as townships that share a boundary (Rook), a corner (Bishop) or either (Queen).
- **Distance band:** Defines neighbours as all townships within a fixed distance.
- **K-nearest neighbours (KNN):** Defines the neighbours of a township as its k closest townships, based on the distance between township points.

To determine the most appropriate neighbour structure for this study, the distributions generated by the three definitions are evaluated below:

```{r}
nb_q <- st_contiguity(mmr_utm$geometry)
nb_dist <- st_dist_band(mmr_utm$geometry)
nb_knn5 <- st_knn(mmr_utm$geometry, k = 5)

bind_rows(tibble(neighbours = "Queen contiguity", n = spdep::card(nb_q)),
          tibble(neighbours = "Distance band", n = spdep::card(nb_dist)),
          tibble(neighbours = "KNN", n = spdep::card(nb_knn5))) %>%
  group_by(neighbours) %>%
  summarise(min = min(n), median = median(n), max = max(n),
            no_neighbours = sum(n == 0))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Based on the results, Queen contiguity leaves three townships entirely without any neighbours, while a fixed distance band creates extreme variance ranging from 1 to 104 neighbours. KNN gives every township exactly 5 neighbours.
:::

For this study, **KNN** is used because it ensures every township has neighbours by construction, allowing direct control over the neighbour count. In contrast, contiguity relies on shared borders, which can leave isolated townships without any neighbours. A fixed distance band is also not ideal as township sizes across Myanmar differ and a single distance band generates widely varying neighbour counts.

The value k = 5 is chosen because it matches the median number of Queen contiguity neighbours. A relatively small k also keeps the neighbourhood local, since a larger k includes more distant townships and dilutes local patterns.

#### 7.1.3 Choice of Weights

Weights can be assigned in several ways:

- **Binary:** Neighbours receive a weight of 1 and all other townships a weight of 0.
- **Row-standardised:** The weights of each township are scaled to sum to 1, so each neighbour receives a weight of 1 divided by the number of neighbours.
- **Distance decay:** Closer neighbours receive larger weights, using the inverse of the distance or a kernel function.

Row-standardised weights (`style = "W"`) are used for Moran's I because they convert the spatial lag into an average of the neighbours' values, allowing for a direct comparison with the township's own event count.

The weights are built on the KNN neighbours:

```{r}
wm_knn <- mmr_utm %>%
  mutate(nb = st_knn(geometry, k = 5),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

wm_knn$wt[[1]]
```

With five neighbours per township, each neighbour receives a weight of 0.2.

### 7.2 Global Moran's I

Global Moran's I assesses the spatial dependence of political violence events across townships, analysing the total event counts on their original scale. If the events are randomly distributed across townships, Moran's I will indicate no significant spatial autocorrelation.

The test evaluates the following hypotheses:

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** Political violence events are randomly distributed across townships.
- **Alternative hypothesis (H1):** There is spatial autocorrelation, indicating that townships with similar event counts are clustered (positive) or dispersed (negative).

The test is conducted at the 5% significance level (p \< 0.05).

#### 7.2.1 Global Moran's I Test and Permutation Test

```{r}
global_moran_test(wm_knn$events, 
                  wm_knn$nb, 
                  wm_knn$wt,
                  alternative = "two.sided")
```

```{r}
gmoran <- global_moran_perm(wm_knn$events, 
                            wm_knn$nb, 
                            wm_knn$wt,
                            alternative = "two.sided", 
                            nsim = 99)
gmoran
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
From the outputs above, the following statistical inferences are drawn:

- Moran's I statistic: 0.450 (Expectation: -0.003)
- Standard deviate: 14.075
- p-value (Moran's I test): \< 2.2e-16
- p-value (Monte Carlo Permutation test): \< 2.2e-16
- Permutation test rank: 100 out of 100

The Global Moran's I statistic of 0.450 sits well above its expectation, indicating positive spatial autocorrelation. Both the Moran's I test and the Monte Carlo permutation test return low p-values (p \< 0.05). Hence, the null hypothesis is rejected at the 5% significance level, providing strong evidence that townships with similar political violence event counts tend to be located near each other. However, as the global statistic does not identify where the clusters are located, it will need to be examined using local measures.
:::

#### 7.2.2 Visualising Monte Carlo Simulation of Global Moran's I

The simulated Moran's I values from the permutation test are plotted as a histogram, with the observed statistic marked by a red line.

```{r}
hist(gmoran$res,
     main = "Histogram of Global Moran's I Monte-Carlo Simulation Results",
     xlab = "Moran's I", ylab = "Frequency")
abline(v = gmoran$statistic, col = "red")
```

## 8 Local Measures of Spatial Association

The global statistic shows that clustering exists, but it does not identify where these clusters are located. Local measures are calculated for each township, which allows clusters to be mapped.

Two measures are applied: 

- **Local Moran's I**: Identifies clusters and outliers of similar or dissimilar event counts 
- **Local Gi**\*: Identifies hot spots and cold spots

### 8.1 Local Moran's I

Local Moran's I is a Local Indicator of Spatial Association (LISA). It compares the event count of each township with the weighted average of its neighbours' counts. Townships with a significant result are classified into one of four LISA types:

- **High-High**: a township with a high count surrounded by townships with high counts (cluster)
- **Low-Low**: a township with a low count surrounded by townships with low counts (cluster)
- **High-Low**: a township with a high count surrounded by townships with low counts (outlier)
- **Low-High**: a township with a low count surrounded by townships with high counts (outlier)

```{r}
lisa <- wm_knn %>%
  mutate(local_moran = local_moran(events, nb, wt, nsim = 99),
         .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
lisa
```

**sfdep** provides three classifications of the LISA type (`mean`, `median` and `pysal`). Since the event counts are right-skewed, the classification could change which townships are labelled high or low, so the number of significant townships in each type is compared below.

```{r}
lisa %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(p_ii_sim < 0.05) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(mean, median, pysal),
               names_to = "classification", values_to = "type") %>%
  count(classification, type)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Given that the three classifications produce identical cluster counts, the `mean` classification is used for subsequent analysis.
:::

#### 8.1.1 Visualising the LISA Map

The LISA map shows only townships with a significant result (p \< 0.05). Townships without a significant result are shaded in grey.

```{r}
lisa_sig <- lisa %>%
  filter(p_ii_sim < 0.05) %>%
  mutate(mean = factor(mean, levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low",
                                        "High-Low", "Low-High")))

tmap_mode("view")

tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "black", lwd = 0.2,
              id = "TS", popup.vars = c("DT", "ST", "events")) +
tm_shape(lisa_sig) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "mean",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = c("#d7191c", "#2c7bb6", "#fdae61", "#abd9e9")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "LISA type"),
              col = "black", lwd = 0.2,
              id = "TS", popup.vars = c("DT", "ST", "events", "mean"))

tmap_mode("plot")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The map shows 61 Low-Low, 25 High-High, and 2 Low-High townships, with no High-Low townships.

- **High-High clusters** are concentrated primarily in the central part of the country, with smaller groups in the north and along the narrow southern strip. These are townships with high event counts surrounded by townships with high counts.
- **Low-Low clusters** cover the north, a large area in the east, the south-west and a small area in the centre. These areas have low event counts across neighbouring townships.
- **Low-High spatial outliers** consist of just two townships. These areas possess low event counts but are surrounded by high-count neighbours. Both outliers are situated next to a High-High cluster.

Townships shaded in grey exhibit no statistically significant local spatial autocorrelation. The townships in each type are examined in Section 8.1.2.
:::

#### 8.1.2 LISA Clusters and Outliers by Township

The High-High townships are listed below:

```{r}
lisa_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(mean == "High-High") %>%
  arrange(desc(events)) %>%
  mutate(ii = round(ii, 3)) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, events, ii, p_ii_sim) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The 25 High-High townships form three geographic groups. The largest is the central cluster spanning Sagaing, Magway, and Mandalay. Within this group, Monywa (1,058 events) and Myaing (936 events) record the highest concentration of political violence and strongest spatial associations of violence.

Beyond this central cluster, a smaller group of three townships (Launglon, Yebyu, and Thayetchaung) lies in Tanintharyi in the south, while Myitkyina in Kachin stands alone in the north. Myitkyina (Kachin) and Tilin (Magway) exhibit the weakest spatial associations of violence.
:::

Due to the high volume of Low-Low townships, they are aggregated at the state and regional level.

```{r}
lisa_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(mean == "Low-Low") %>%
  count(ST, name = "townships") %>%
  arrange(desc(townships)) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The 61 Low-Low townships form four clusters:

- **South Region (27 townships):** Spanning across Yangon (14) and Ayeyarwady (13)
- **East Region (22 townships):** Located in Shan State, comprising of Shan (East), Shan (North), and Shan (South)
- **Central Region (6 townships):** Comprising Nay Pyi Taw (6) and Mandalay (1)
- **North Region (5 townships):** Located in Kachin
:::

The spatial outliers are presented below, detailing individual township counts and their corresponding neighbourhood averages (`neighbour_mean`).

```{r}
lisa %>%
  mutate(neighbour_mean = round(st_lag(events, nb, wt), 1)) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(p_ii_sim < 0.05, mean %in% c("High-Low", "Low-High")) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, events, neighbour_mean, mean, p_ii_sim) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Both spatial outliers are Low-High townships. Mogaung in Kachin records 77 events against a neighbour average of 428.4, while Kalewa in Sagaing records 30 events against a neighbour average of 342.0. This indicates that they are relatively calm townships surrounded by high-violence neighbours. While the data cannot confirm whether this reflects genuinely lower levels of political violence or simply under-reporting, their proximity to active violence areas makes them crucial areas to monitor.

In addition, the absence of High-Low outliers indicates that no high-violence township stands alone among low-violence neighbours. This suggests that political violence does not appear as isolated spikes, but rather spreads across adjacent townships, reinforcing the clustering trends identified by the Global Moran's I statistic.
:::

### 8.2 Local Gi\*

Local Gi\* measures whether a township and its neighbours together have higher or lower event counts than expected by chance. While Local Moran's I identifies specific clusters and outliers, Local Gi\* identifies hot spots and cold spots.

A significant positive Gi\* value indicates a hot spot (high counts around the township), and a significant negative value indicates a cold spot (low counts around it).

The test evaluates the following hypotheses:

- **Null Hypothesis (H0)**: High or low event counts are not concentrated around the township.
- **Alternative Hypothesis (H1)**: High event counts (hot spot) or low event counts (cold spot) are concentrated around the township.

The test is conducted at the 5% significance level (p \< 0.05), using the `local_gstar_perm()` function from the **sfdep** package.

#### 8.2.1 Spatial Weights for Gi\*

The neighbourhood of each township consists of its five nearest townships and the township itself. Inverse distance weights are used, so that nearer townships carry more weight than farther ones, which reflects the idea that nearby places are more related than distant ones (Tobler, 1970). The distances are in metres, since the boundaries are projected to UTM zone 47N.

```{r}
wm_idw <- mmr_utm %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_knn(geometry, k = 5)),
         wts = st_inverse_distance(nb, geometry, scale = 1, alpha = 1),
         .before = 1)
```

#### 8.2.2 Local Gi\* Test

The `local_gstar_perm()` function returns the standardised statistic (`gi_star`) and the simulation-based p-value (`p_sim`) for each township. Townships with p \< 0.05 are retained, and the sign of `gi_star` statistic determines the classification, where positive values indicate hot spots and negative values indicate cold spots.

```{r}
gi <- wm_idw %>%
  mutate(local_gi = local_gstar_perm(events, nb, wts, nsim = 99)) %>%
  unnest(local_gi)

gi_sig <- gi %>%
  filter(p_sim < 0.05) %>%
  mutate(type = factor(if_else(gi_star > 0, "Hot spot", "Cold spot"),
                       levels = c("Hot spot", "Cold spot")))

gi_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(type)
```

#### 8.2.3 Visualising the Gi\* Map

The map shows only townships identified as statistically significant hot spots or cold spots (p \< 0.05). Townships without a significant result are shaded in grey.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

tm_shape(gi) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "black", lwd = 0.2) +
tm_shape(gi_sig) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "type",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = c("#d7191c", "#2c7bb6")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Gi* type"),
              col = "black", lwd = 0.2)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The map shows 24 statistically significant hot spots and 62 cold spots.

- **Hot spots** are concentrated primarily in one large cluster in the central region, with two smaller groups along the narrow southern strip. In these townships and their contiguous neighbourhoods, event counts are significantly higher than expected by random chance.
- **Cold spots** are more geographically extensive, covering the northern tip, a large area in the east, the south-west, and a small area in the centre. In these regions, event counts are significantly lower than expected.

The hot and cold spots cover largely the same areas as the High-High and Low-Low clusters from Local Moran's I, demonstrating a high degree of spatial consistency between the two methodologies. It is important to note that the analysis identifies where high or low counts are concentrated, but does not identify the underlying socio-political reasons for these distributions.
:::

### 8.3 Hot Spots and Cold Spots by Conflict Phase

Section 8.2 treats the whole study period as one snapshot. To see how hot spots and cold spots shift as the conflict develops, Local Gi\* is computed separately for each of the three phases defined in Section 3.2.

#### 8.3.1 Events by Phase

The events of each township are summed within each phase, and the phases are summarised below.

```{r}
phase_levels <- c("Coup and crackdown", "Armed resistance", "After Operation 1027")

pv_phase <- pv_tm %>%
  mutate(phase = case_when(month < as.Date("2021-09-01") ~ phase_levels[1],
                           month < as.Date("2023-11-01") ~ phase_levels[2],
                           TRUE ~ phase_levels[3]),
         phase = factor(phase, levels = phase_levels)) %>%
  group_by(phase, TS_PCODE) %>%
  summarise(events = sum(events), months = n_distinct(month), .groups = "drop")

pv_phase %>%
  group_by(phase) %>%
  summarise(months = first(months),
            townships_with_events = sum(events > 0),
            events = sum(events),
            events_per_month = round(events / months))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Political violence intensifies across the phases, rising from an average of 464 events per month during the coup and crackdown, to 992 during the armed resistance, and reaching 1,078 after Operation 1027 (which is more than double the rate of the first phase).

The number of townships recording at least one event rises from 264 in the first phase to 315 in the second (encompassing nearly all of Myanmar's 330 townships), before stabilizing at 313 after Operation 1027. This indicates that political violence spread spatially to most of the country during the armed resistance phase, whereas the subsequent spike in violence after Operation 1027 was driven by intensification within already-affected townships.
:::

#### 8.3.2 Local Gi\* by Phase

Local Gi\* is computed for each phase with the same neighbours, weights and number of simulations as in Section 8.2. As Gi\* compares each township with the national average within the same phase, the results are comparable across phases of different lengths.

```{r}
gi_phase <- map_dfr(phase_levels, function(p) {
  set.seed(123)
  wm_idw %>%
    select(TS_PCODE, TS, DT, ST, nb, wts) %>%
    left_join(pv_phase %>% filter(phase == p) %>% select(TS_PCODE, events),
              by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
    mutate(local_gi = local_gstar_perm(events, nb, wts, nsim = 99)) %>%
    unnest(local_gi) %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(TS_PCODE, TS, DT, ST, events, gi_star, p_sim) %>%
    mutate(phase = factor(p, levels = phase_levels),
           type = case_when(p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
                            p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot",
                            TRUE ~ "Not significant"))
})

gi_phase %>%
  count(phase, type) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The number of statistically significant townships rises from 31 in the first phase to 80 and 84 in the subsequent phases, indicating that the spatial pattern of political violence becomes much clearer as the conflict progresses.

Hot spots peak during the armed resistance (31) but fall after Operation 1027 (16), even though the monthly rate of violence is at its highest during this final phase (Section 8.3.1). As Gi* compares each township against the national average within the same phase, this indicates that violence after Operation 1027 is so widespread and elevated that fewer townships stand out significantly above the new baseline. In contrast, cold spots grow steadily, demonstrating that the relatively low-violence areas become more clearly defined in each phase.
:::

#### 8.3.3 Visualising the Phase Maps

The three maps show only townships that are significant hot spots or cold spots (p < 0.05) in each phase. Townships without a significant result are shaded in grey.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7

phase_map <- function(p) {
  d <- mmr_utm %>%
    select(TS_PCODE) %>%
    left_join(gi_phase %>% filter(phase == p), by = "TS_PCODE")

  tm_shape(d) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "black", lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_shape(d %>% filter(type != "Not significant")) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "type",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                  values = c("Hot spot" = "#d7191c", "Cold spot" = "#2c7bb6")),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Gi* type"),
                col = "black", lwd = 0.1) +
    tm_title(p)
}

tmap_arrange(lapply(phase_levels, phase_map), ncol = 3)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The location of the hot spots shifts between phases. During the coup and crackdown, a small group of hot spots lies in the north and north-east. During the armed resistance, a cluster forms in the north-west and along the southern strip. After Operation 1027, the north-western cluster largely disappears, and the remaining hot spots are smaller and scattered across the centre, with a few on the west coast and in the south-east. In contrast, cold spots consolidate into one large block in the east and a growing area in the south.

The whole-period map in Section 8.2 closely resembles the armed resistance phase, which is the longest and contains the most events. Summing the whole period therefore hides the later shift of hot spots away from the north-west, which only becomes visible when the phases are compared.
:::

#### 8.3.4 Hot Spots by Phase and Region

The number of hot spot townships in each state or region is compared across the phases.

```{r}
gi_phase %>%
  filter(type == "Hot spot") %>%
  count(ST, phase) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = phase, values_from = n,
              values_fill = 0, names_sort = TRUE) %>%
  arrange(desc(rowSums(across(where(is.numeric))))) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The large cluster during the armed resistance was heavily concentrated in Sagaing (16) and Magway (5), but this decreases after Operation 1027. Conversely, Bago (East), Kayin, and Rakhine emerge as significant hot spots only in the final phase, demonstrating a shift in the spatial distribution of political violence.
:::

As the final phase reflects the most recent pattern of violence, its hot spot townships are listed below.

```{r}
gi_phase %>%
  filter(type == "Hot spot", phase == "After Operation 1027") %>%
  arrange(desc(gi_star)) %>%
  mutate(gi_star = round(gi_star, 3)) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, events, gi_star, p_sim) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

## 9 Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)

Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) evaluates how hot spots and cold spots change over time. It consists of four steps: building a space-time cube, calculating the Gi\* statistic for each township in each month, testing the temporal trend of the Gi\* values over time with the Mann-Kendall test, and classifying each township based on the trend and statistical significance. EHSA adds the time dimension to the static Gi\* map.

Each township is assigned to one class, based on how many months are significant hot or cold spots (at the 5% level), whether the most recent month is significant, as well as the Mann-Kendall trend.

The classes follow the standard definitions established by Esri (n.d.) for space-time pattern mining. The key classes are as follows:

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Intensifying hot spot | A statistically significant hot spot for at least 90% of the time periods, including the final month, with a significant upward trend in the intensity of clustering |
| Oscillating hot spot | A statistically significant hot spot for the final month, but a statistically significant cold spot in earlier months |
| Sporadic hot spot | An on-and-off hot spot; less than 90% of the time periods are significant hot spots, and it has never been a significant cold spot |
| Persistent cold spot | A statistically significant cold spot for at least 90% of the time periods, with no discernible trend indicating an increase or decrease in clustering intensity |
| Diminishing cold spot | A statistically significant cold spot for at least 90% of the months, including the final month, with a significant upward trend in the Gi\* values (indicating the cold spot is weakening) |
| Oscillating cold spot | A statistically significant cold spot for the final month, but a statistically significant hot spot in earlier months |
| Sporadic cold spot | An on-and-off cold spot; less than 90% of the time periods are significant cold spots, and it has never been a significant hot spot |
| No pattern detected | Does not fall into any of the hot spot or cold spot categories |

### 9.1 Neighbours and Weights in Space and Time

The neighbours and weights from Section 8.2.1 are reused in place of standard Queen contiguity, ensuring that EHSA and the Local Gi\* analysis share the same neighbourhoods. The time lag is set to `k = 1`, allowing the Gi\* value of a township in a month to also use its neighbours' values in the previous month.

```{r}
pv_st <- pv_st %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_knn(geometry, k = 5)),
         wts = st_inverse_distance(nb, geometry, 
                                   scale = 1, alpha = 1)) %>%
  activate("data")
```

### 9.2 Mann-Kendall Test and EHSA

For each township, the Mann-Kendall test examines the series of 57 monthly Gi\* values to check whether it shows a consistent upward or downward trend over time.

The test evaluates the following hypotheses:

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** There is no monotonic trend in the township's Gi\* values over time.
- **Alternative hypothesis (H1):** There is a monotonic trend, indicating that the Gi\* values rise or fall over time.

The tests are conducted at the 5% significance level (p \< 0.05).

`emerging_hotspot_analysis()` calculates the Gi\* of each township in each month:

```{r}
set.seed(123)
ehsa <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(x = pv_st,
                                  .var = "events",
                                  k = 1,
                                  nb_col = "nb",
                                  wt_col = "wts",
                                  nsim = 99,
                                  threshold = 0.05,
                                  include_gi = TRUE)

glimpse(ehsa)
```

The monthly Gi\* values of each township are extracted from the output. The cube is ordered by month and then by township, in the order of the township boundaries.

```{r}
n_locs <- n_distinct(pv_tm$TS_PCODE)
n_times <- n_distinct(pv_tm$month)

gi_month <- attr(ehsa, "gi_star") %>%
  mutate(location = rep(attr(pv_st, "geometry")$TS_PCODE, times = n_times),
         month_id = rep(seq_len(n_times), each = n_locs))
```

#### 9.2.1 Mann-Kendall Trends

The number of townships with a significant trend in Gi\* at the 5% level is shown below:

```{r}
mmr_trend <- mmr_utm %>%
  left_join(ehsa %>% select(location, tau, p_value),
            by = c("TS_PCODE" = "location")) %>%
  mutate(trend = case_when(p_value < 0.05 & tau > 0 ~ "Significant increase",
                           p_value < 0.05 & tau < 0 ~ "Significant decrease",
                           TRUE ~ "No significant trend"))

mmr_trend %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(trend)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Of the 330 townships, 203 (61.5%) have a significant trend in their Gi\* values, hence the null hypothesis is rejected. 98 townships (29.7%) show a significant increase and 105 (31.8%) show a significant decrease, while the null hypothesis is not rejected for the remaining 127 (38.5%).
:::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

tm_shape(mmr_trend) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "black", lwd = 0.2) +
tm_shape(mmr_trend %>% filter(trend != "No significant trend")) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "trend",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = c("Significant increase" = "#7b3294",
                           "Significant decrease" = "#008837")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Mann-Kendall trend"),
              col = "black", lwd = 0.2)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The map shows a clear split between north and south. Significant decreases dominate a broad band across the north-west and the upper centre, with smaller groups in the far north. Significant increases cover the south-west and lower centre, a block in the east, and the narrow southern strip. Relative to the rest of the country, the concentration of violence is therefore moving away from the north-west and upper centre, towards the south and the east.

These trends are relative, not absolute. The Gi\* of each month is measured against the national average for that month, so a rising or falling trend shows how a township's neighbourhood changes compared with the rest of the country, not necessarily a change in the absolute number of events. A rising Gi\* also has two readings: For a hot spot, violence is becoming more concentrated. On the other hand, for a cold spot, the cold spot is weakening.
:::

#### 9.2.2 Rate of Change (Sen's Slope)

The Mann-Kendall statistic (`tau`) shows how consistently a township's Gi\* rises or falls, but not how fast. The rate of change is therefore estimated using Sen's slope (Sen, 1968), the median of the slopes between every pair of months in a township's Gi\* series. As it uses the median, it is not skewed by extreme values, making it the standard measure of trend size paired with the Mann-Kendall test. The slope is calculated per month and multiplied by 12 to give the change in Gi\* per year.

```{r}
pairs <- combn(n_times, 2)

sen_slope <- function(y) {
  median((y[pairs[2, ]] - y[pairs[1, ]]) / (pairs[2, ] - pairs[1, ]))
}

sen <- gi_month %>%
  arrange(location, month_id) %>%
  group_by(location) %>%
  summarise(sen_per_year = round(sen_slope(gi_star) * 12, 3))

sen_tbl <- mmr_trend %>%
  left_join(sen, by = c("TS_PCODE" = "location"))
```

The rate of change is summarised for each trend direction:

```{r}
sen_tbl %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(trend) %>%
  summarise(townships = n(),
            median = median(sen_per_year),
            min = min(sen_per_year),
            max = max(sen_per_year))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
Sen's slope aligns with the Mann-Kendall results. All 105 townships with a significant decrease have a negative slope, and all 98 with a significant increase have a positive one. In areas where the concentration of political violence is falling, it decreases at a median rate of 0.333 per year, slightly faster than the median rise of 0.267 per year in areas where it is increasing.

Over the entire study period, a typical change of about 0.3 per year translates to a shift of approximately 1.4 in Gi\*. This is a substantial change, as Gi\* values beyond about +/- 1.96 are usually significant at the 5% level. A shift of 1.4 is therefore large enough to move a previously average township close to becoming a significant hot or cold spot.

The townships without a significant trend have a median slope close to zero (0.007), yet some may still reach -0.96 or 0.463 per year. In such cases, the Gi\* changes considerably but not consistently, which is why the Mann-Kendall test does not confirm a trend. Sen's slope therefore complements the Mann-Kendall test.
:::

The townships with a significant trend are mapped below by their rate of change. Purple shows a rising Gi\* and green shows a falling one, and darker shades indicate faster change. Townships without a significant trend are shaded in grey.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

tm_shape(sen_tbl) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "black", lwd = 0.2) +
tm_shape(sen_tbl %>% filter(trend != "No significant trend")) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "sen_per_year",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty",
                                              values = "-brewer.prgn",
                                              midpoint = 0),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Change in Gi* per year"),
              col = "black", lwd = 0.2)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The fastest changes are concentrated in a few places:

- The steepest declines form a compact core in the north-west and upper centre, corresponding to the large hot spot cluster from the armed resistance phase (Section 8.3). There is another group in the south-east.
- The steepest increases are dispersed, occurring in single townships scattered across the central, southern, and western regions.
:::

The 10 fastest-rising and 10 fastest-falling townships are listed below:

```{r}
sen_tbl %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(trend == "Significant increase") %>%
  slice_max(sen_per_year, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(tau = round(tau, 3)) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, tau, sen_per_year) %>%
  knitr::kable()

sen_tbl %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(trend == "Significant decrease") %>%
  slice_min(sen_per_year, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(tau = round(tau, 3)) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, tau, sen_per_year) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The fastest rises are spread across six states, led by Kyaukme in Shan (North) and Kyauktaga in Bago (East). Six of the ten (Kyaukme, Kyauktaga, Myeik, Myawaddy, Pyinoolwin and Mogoke) are also hot spots after Operation 1027 (Section 8.3.4), indicating that violence is building fastest where it is already concentrated. The other four (Hpapun, Kyaukkyi, Ramree, and Munaung) are rising quickly without yet being hot spots, which marks them as critical townships to monitor.

The fastest declines are concentrated in Sagaing, which has seven of the eleven townships (due to a tie at 10th position), led by Budalin. This highlights that the primary hot spot cluster from the armed resistance phase is easing faster than anywhere else.
:::

#### 9.2.3 Checking the Classes

For each township, the number of months in which it is a significant cold spot or hot spot is counted, and the townships labelled "intensifying hotspot" are listed:

```{r}
sig_months <- gi_month %>%
  group_by(location) %>%
  summarise(cold_months = sum(p_sim <= 0.05 & gi_star < 0),
            hot_months = sum(p_sim <= 0.05 & gi_star > 0))

ehsa %>%
  filter(classification == "intensifying hotspot") %>%
  left_join(sig_months, by = "location") %>%
  left_join(mmr_events %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST, events),
            by = c("location" = "TS_PCODE")) %>%
  select(TS, ST, events, tau, p_value, cold_months, hot_months)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Classification check"}
`emerging_hotspot_analysis()` of **sfdep** labels 10 townships as "intensifying hotspot", but the table above shows that they are significant cold spots in almost every month (>90%), with at most one significant hot month, and record very few events. The **sfdep** rule for "intensifying hotspot" counts significant months without checking whether they are hot or cold. These townships meet every condition of the "diminishing coldspot" rule: a significant cold spot for at least 90% of the months, a significant final month, and a significant upward trend. Therefore, they are relabelled as **diminishing cold spots**. Only the class name changes, while the other fields remain unchanged.
:::

To correct this, the relabelling explicitly checks for the 90% cold spot condition. This ensures that any genuine intensifying hot spots retain their correct label.

```{r}
ehsa <- ehsa %>%
  left_join(sig_months, by = "location") %>%
  mutate(classification = if_else(classification == "intensifying hotspot" &
                                    cold_months >= 0.9 * n_times,
                                  "diminishing coldspot",
                                  classification)) %>%
  select(-cold_months, -hot_months)
```

#### 9.2.4 Distribution of EHSA Classes

The number of townships in each class is shown below:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

ehsa_cols <- c("intensifying hotspot" = "#b2182b",
               "oscilating hotspot"   = "#f46d43",
               "sporadic hotspot"     = "#fdae61",
               "diminishing coldspot" = "#5ab4ac",
               "persistent coldspot"  = "#2166ac",
               "oscilating coldspot"  = "#4393c3",
               "sporadic coldspot"    = "#92c5de",
               "no pattern detected"  = "grey70")

ehsa %>%
  count(classification) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = reorder(classification, n), fill = classification)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.2, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ehsa_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "Number of townships", y = NULL)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The 330 townships fall into seven classes. 126 townships (38.2%) are sporadic cold spots and 123 (37.3%) show no pattern. Hot spot classes cover 47 townships (14.2%): 35 oscillating and 12 sporadic. The other cold spot classes cover 34 townships (10.3%): 16 oscillating, 10 diminishing and 8 persistent.
:::

### 9.3 EHSA Map

The EHSA results are joined to the township boundaries, and only townships with a significant Mann-Kendall trend (p < 0.05) and an assigned EHSA class are shown. Townships without a significant trend or without a detected pattern are shaded in grey. By definition, persistent cold spots lack a significant trend and are excluded from this map.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

mmr_ehsa <- mmr_utm %>%
  left_join(ehsa, by = c("TS_PCODE" = "location"))

ehsa_sig <- mmr_ehsa %>%
  filter(p_value < 0.05, classification != "no pattern detected") %>%
  mutate(classification = factor(classification,
                                 levels = intersect(names(ehsa_cols), classification)))

tm_shape(mmr_ehsa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "black", lwd = 0.2) +
tm_shape(ehsa_sig) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "classification",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = unname(ehsa_cols[levels(ehsa_sig$classification)])),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "EHSA class"),
              col = "black", lwd = 0.2)
```

The number of townships in each class shown on the map:

```{r}
ehsa_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(classification)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The map shows 120 townships with a significant trend and an EHSA class. Cold spots classes (95 townships) dominate, mainly in the south-west and east region. In contrast, the 25 hot spots are highly scattered, mostly along the edges of the country - the west coast, the far north and the southern strip.

Overall, the hot spots are highly fragmented; they do not form a single stable core, which reflects the absence of persistent or intensifying hot spots in the data.

Each class is further examined by township in Section 9.4.
:::

### 9.4 EHSA Classes by Township

The townships in each class shown on the map are examined below, starting with the hot spot classes. Each table lists the townships by their total number of events over the period, with the Mann-Kendall statistic (`tau`) and its p-value.

#### 9.4.1 Oscillating Hot Spots

Oscillating hot spots are hot spots in the final month after being significant cold spots in at least one earlier month, making them the most critical class for current peace-building efforts.

```{r}
ehsa_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(classification == "oscilating hotspot") %>%
  arrange(desc(events)) %>%
  mutate(tau = round(tau, 3),
         p_value = signif(p_value, 3)) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, events, tau, p_value) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The 20 oscillating hot spots are spread across 10 states and regions. Rakhine has the most townships in this class (Ann, Buthidaung, Toungup and Ramree), followed by Tanintharyi (Palaw, Dawei and Myeik), Kayah (Loikaw, Hpruso and Shadaw) and Sagaing (Budalin, Mingin and Nanyun). These are primarily high conflict areas, where 13 of the townships record over 200 events.

The trend separates these hot spots into two distinct groups:

- **Rising concentration (13 townships):** These areas show a rising Gi\*, indicating violence has become increasingly concentrated. The townships with the most consistent upward trends are in Rakhine (Ann, Toungup and Ramree; tau > 0.53), in Bago (East) (Kyauktaga; tau = 0.492) and in Kayin (Myawaddy; tau = 0.477).
- **Easing concentration (7 townships):** These areas show a falling Gi\*, which includes three townships in Kayah and three in Sagaing. 
Even though they remain hot spots in the final month, their concentration of violence has decreased relative to the rest of the country.
:::

#### 9.4.2 Sporadic Hot Spots

Sporadic hot spots experience intermittent spikes in violence, without becoming significant cold spots.

```{r}
ehsa_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(classification == "sporadic hotspot") %>%
  arrange(desc(events)) %>%
  mutate(tau = round(tau, 3),
         p_value = signif(p_value, 3)) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, events, tau, p_value) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The 5 sporadic hot spots lie in Shan (North) (Muse and Hseni), Mandalay (Mogoke), Kayin (Hlaingbwe), and Kayah (Mese). These townships have been hot spots in some months but never significant cold spots, which indicates that violence in these areas fluctuates without the area ever becoming calm relative to the rest of the country.

The trend separates the hot spots into two groups:

- **Rising concentration (2 townships):** Mogoke (tau = 0.437) and Hlaingbwe (0.192) have a rising Gi\*, with Mogoke showing the most consistent upward trend in this class. 
- **Easing concentration (3 townships):** Muse (which records the most events of 648), Hseni and Mese have a falling Gi*. The violence around them has become less concentrated over the period.

Interestingly, Mese records only 27 events. This demonstrates that a township can be flagged as a hot spot due to intense violence in its neighbouring areas rather than just within its own borders.
:::

#### 9.4.3 Diminishing Cold Spots

Diminishing cold spots are significant cold spots in almost every month, with a rising Gi\* over the period.

```{r}
ehsa_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(classification == "diminishing coldspot") %>%
  arrange(desc(events)) %>%
  mutate(tau = round(tau, 3),
         p_value = signif(p_value, 3)) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, events, tau, p_value) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
All 10 diminishing cold spots are located in Shan: six in Shan (East), three in Shan (North), and one in Shan (South). These townships are among the least active in the country, recording between 0 and 18 events over the entire period.

However, these cold spots exhibit a rising Gi* (tau ranging from 0.180 to 0.253). As a township's Gi* score incorporates neighbouring spatial data, this rising trend reflects escalating violence in adjacent townships. Hence, these areas remain critical to monitor, as their relative stability may soon be compromised by encroaching violence.
:::

#### 9.4.4 Oscillating Cold Spots

Oscillating cold spots are areas that were significant hot spots previously but transitioned to significant cold spots by the final month.

```{r}
ehsa_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(classification == "oscilating coldspot") %>%
  arrange(desc(events)) %>%
  mutate(tau = round(tau, 3),
         p_value = signif(p_value, 3)) %>%
  select(TS, DT, ST, events, tau, p_value) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The 13 oscillating cold spots are heavily concentrated in two regions: Mandalay and Shan (North).

With the exception of Mongnai (tau = 0.179), all townships in this class exhibit a falling Gi*. The most consistent downward trends occurred in Mandalay and Sagaing. In these areas, the relative concentration of violence has dropped sharply. Meanwhile, the five townships in Shan (North) show less consistent but still significant downward trends.

In contrast to oscillating hot spots, this class represents areas where violence was previously highly concentrated but has since eased.
:::

#### 9.4.5 Sporadic Cold Spots

Given the large number of sporadic cold spots, they are summarised by state and region along with their trend directions.

```{r}
ehsa_sig %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(classification == "sporadic coldspot") %>%
  count(ST, trend = if_else(tau > 0, "Rising", "Falling")) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = trend, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-ST))) %>%
  arrange(desc(Total)) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The 72 sporadic cold spots span eight states and regions. Yangon accounts for 39 of them, though this high count is partly because the city is divided into numerous small urban townships. These are areas that experience intermittent periods as significant cold spots but never escalate into significant hot spots.

- **Rising concentration (25 townships):** Concentrated mainly in Bago(West), Magway, and Mandalay, where a rising Gi* signals that these quiet areas are becoming more active relative to the rest of the country.
- **Easing concentration (47 townships):** Predominantly located in Yangon (38 townships), where a falling Gi* indicates the relative intensity of violence continues to steadily decline.
:::

## 10 Integrated Findings

This section brings together the local measures (Section 8), the conflict phases (Section 8.3) and the Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (Section 9) to show the full picture of where political violence is concentrated, how it has shifted and where it is heading.

### 10.1 Agreement Between the Local Measures

As Local Moran's I and Local Gi\* measure local clustering in different ways, areas identified by both methods ensure that the clusters do not depend on the choice of method.

The LISA type of each township is compared with its Gi\* result:

```{r}
lisa %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(TS_PCODE,
            lisa = if_else(p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Not significant")) %>%
  left_join(gi %>%
              st_drop_geometry() %>%
              transmute(TS_PCODE,
                        gi = case_when(p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
                                       p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot",
                                       TRUE ~ "Not significant")),
            by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  count(lisa, gi) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = gi, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The two measures show strong agreement, indicating that the identified clusters are robust and do not depend on the choice of method. 

21 of the 25 High-High townships (84%) identified by Local Moran's I are also Gi\* hot spots, and 55 of the 61 Low-Low townships (90%) align as cold spots. Furthermore, there are no contradictions, as no High-High township is classified as a cold spot and no Low-Low township as a hot spot.
:::

### 10.2 How the Pattern Shifts Across Phases

Both the phase maps (Section 8.3) and the monthly trends (Section 9.2) capture the same geographic shift in the conflict. Following Operation 1027, the previously dense hot spot cluster in Sagaing begins to shrink, which is directly reflected by the steepest falling trends in the monthly data. New hot spots also appear in scattered townships, matching the locations of the fastest-rising monthly trends.

As the armed resistance phase was the longest and contains the most events, it dominates the whole-period Gi\* map. As a result, the whole-period map understates how far the geographical pattern of violence has already shifted. To accurately understand the current situation, the final phase map and the monthly trends provide a much better representation than the whole-period baseline.

### 10.3 Where the Evidence Converges

To bring the evidence together, townships are grouped into four types. The rules are applied in order, so each township belongs to at most one type:

| Type | Rule |
|---|---|
| Escalating hot spot | A hot spot after Operation 1027 (Section 8.3) with a significant rising trend (Section 9.2) |
| Emerging hot spot | Not a hot spot after Operation 1027 and not an EHSA cold spot class, but rising at 0.5 or more per year |
| Fading hot spot | A hot spot over the whole period (Section 8.2) with a significant falling trend |
| Weakening cold spot | An EHSA cold spot class with a significant rising trend |

A rate of 0.5 per year adds up to about 2.4 in Gi\* over the study period, enough to move an average township beyond the usual significance threshold of about 1.96 (p < 0.05).

```{r}
phase3_hot <- gi_phase %>%
  filter(phase == "After Operation 1027", type == "Hot spot") %>%
  pull(TS_PCODE)

static_hot <- gi_sig %>%
  filter(type == "Hot spot") %>%
  pull(TS_PCODE)

type_levels <- c("Escalating hot spot", "Emerging hot spot",
                 "Fading hot spot", "Weakening cold spot")

typology <- sen_tbl %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  left_join(ehsa %>% select(location, classification),
            by = c("TS_PCODE" = "location")) %>%
  mutate(cold_class = str_detect(classification, "coldspot"),
         type = case_when(
           TS_PCODE %in% phase3_hot & trend == "Significant increase" ~ type_levels[1],
           !(TS_PCODE %in% phase3_hot) & trend == "Significant increase" &
             sen_per_year >= 0.5 & !cold_class ~ type_levels[2],
           TS_PCODE %in% static_hot & trend == "Significant decrease" ~ type_levels[3],
           cold_class & trend == "Significant increase" ~ type_levels[4]),
         type = factor(type, levels = type_levels)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(type))
```

The number of townships in each type, their main states and regions, and the fastest-changing townships are summarised below.

```{r}
typology %>%
  arrange(type, desc(abs(sen_per_year))) %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  summarise(townships = n(),
            main_regions = paste(
              names(sort(table(ST), 
                         decreasing = TRUE))[1:min(3, n_distinct(ST))],
              collapse = ", "),
            fastest_changing = paste(head(TS, 5), collapse = ", ")) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The evidence categorises 67 townships into the four types. Only 8 townships are classified as escalating hot spots (Kyaukme and Kyauktaga), while almost twice as many are classified as emerging hot spots (primarily in Bago (East), Rakhine and Tanintharyi). This indicates that more townships are on the verge of becoming hot spots than are already entrenched in escalating violence. Notably, Bago (East) appears in both categories, highlighting it as an expanding zone of conflict.

The "fading hot spot" category is small and confined to just 8 townships in Sagaing and Magway. The largest category is "weakening cold spot" (36 townships), mainly located in Bago (West), Magway, and Mandalay. As Magway appears in both fading hot spot and weakening cold spot, this suggests that violence may be spreading outward from the former core into neighbouring areas that had been relatively calm.
:::

### 10.4 When the Change Happens

The Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen's slope summarise each township's 57 months in a single value, so they do not show when the change happened. To see how the conflict developed over time, the township with the largest Sen's slope is selected from each type.

```{r}
reps <- typology %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  mutate(townships_in_type = n()) %>%
  slice_max(abs(sen_per_year), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

reps %>%
  select(type, townships_in_type, TS, DT, ST, sen_per_year) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

The monthly Gi\* of these four townships is shown below, with the three conflict phases shaded in the background. Values above zero mean that violence around the township is more concentrated than the national average in that month, and values below zero mean that it is less concentrated.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6.5

month_dates <- seq(as.Date("2021-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = n_times)

phases <- tibble(start = as.Date(c("2021-01-01", "2021-09-01", "2023-11-01")),
                 end   = as.Date(c("2021-09-01", "2023-11-01", "2025-10-01")),
                 phase = factor(phase_levels, levels = phase_levels))

panels <- reps %>%
  transmute(location = TS_PCODE, panel = paste0(type, ": ", TS))

gi_month %>%
  inner_join(panels, by = "location") %>%
  mutate(month = month_dates[month_id],
         panel = factor(panel, levels = panels$panel)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = gi_star)) +
  geom_rect(data = phases,
            aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = phase),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#fee0d2", "#e5f5e0", "#deebf7"), name = "Phase") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Monthly Gi*") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Analysis"}
The timing of the shift in political violence differs across the four townships. Kyaukme, the fastest escalating hot spot, stays close to zero for most of the first two phases. It mainly rises after Operation 1027, reaching its highest peaks in 2024 and 2025. Hpapun, the fastest emerging hot spot, starts to build up during the armed resistance phase and keeps rising after Operation 1027.

On the other hand, Budalin (the fastest fading hot spot) already shows a sharp rise during the coup and crackdown. It peaks in early 2022 and then declines steadily through the armed resistance. This shows that the fading of the former core was well underway long before Operation 1027 even began. Finally, Kyaukpadaung, the fastest weakening cold spot, stays below zero for most of the study period and only moves into positive values after Operation 1027.

Overall, this suggests that the escalation of the newest hot spots is concentrated mainly after Operation 1027, whereas the decline of the former hot spots began much earlier.
:::
